introduction: On this Sunday, Isaiah tells Jerusalem that God delights in her as a bridegroom rejoices in his bride. In the Gospel, at the wedding at Cana, Mary notices that the wine has run out and tells the servants, Do whatever he tells you. Jesus changes water into wine, the first of his signs. Paul speaks of the many gifts given by the one Spirit. Let us bring our needs to Jesus with Mary's trust.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord rejoices over us as a bridegroom rejoices over his bride. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may use the many gifts of the Spirit for the good of all. Let us pray to the Lord.
For married couples, especially those whose love has run dry: that Christ may renew their joy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who feel forsaken or desolate: that they may know that God delights in them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those whose needs no one notices: that, like Mary, we may see and bring them to Jesus. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may do whatever Jesus tells us. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, at Cana your Son revealed his glory and his disciples believed in him. Fill our lives with the new wine of his love, and help us to do whatever he tells us. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: They have no wine
reflection.body:
Isaiah uses the language of love and marriage to describe God's relationship with his people. Jerusalem had been called "Forsaken" and "Desolate," but God gives her a new name, "for the LORD delights in you." And he adds: "As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so your God will rejoice over you."

It is fitting, then, that Jesus' first sign in John's Gospel takes place at a wedding. In the middle of the celebration, the wine runs out, a serious embarrassment for the young couple. Mary notices. She simply tells Jesus, "They have no wine." His answer seems to hold back: "My hour has not yet come." But Mary is confident, and she tells the servants, "Whatever he says to you, do it." These are the last words of Mary recorded in John's Gospel, and they remain her advice to every Christian.

The servants fill six large stone jars with water, "up to the brim." When the head steward tastes it, it has become wine, and better than before: "You have kept the good wine until now!" John tells us that this was "This beginning of his signs," in which Jesus "revealed his glory; and his disciples believed in him."

The sign speaks of abundance. Jesus does not just solve a problem; he gives more than enough, and the best. Where our joy runs out, he brings new wine.

Paul reminds us that God's gifts are given to everyone in different ways: "Now there are various kinds of gifts, but the same Spirit." Each gift is given "for the profit of all."

This week, tell Jesus simply where the wine has run out in your life, as Mary did. Then listen for what he asks of you, and do it, even if it seems as ordinary as filling jars with water.
